name: go-and (bwesterb)
language: Go (AVX2 and NEON assembly, generated with avo)
baseline: naive one-byte-at-a-time Go for loop (and a uint64-wise pure-Go version, build tag purego), both compiled by the Go gc compiler
workload: bitwise and/or/xor/andnot, any-bit-set (masked and unmasked) and popcount (masked and unmasked) over []byte slices, Go benchmarks with -count=10 compared with benchstat
claimed_speedup: Intel i9-13900: geomean time 16.14us naive -> 1.046us asm (-93.52%, about 15x derived from page data); And-32 6942.5ns -> 360.8ns (-94.80%); Xor-32 6996.5ns -> 361.9ns; Popcnt-32 177.46us -> 22.49us (-87.33%); throughput And 4.293GiB/s naive -> 82.618GiB/s asm. Apple M2 Pro (NEON): geomean 30.52us naive -> 1.455us asm (-95.23%).
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain via go test -count=10 (benchmark.sh); asm run vs '-tags purego' vs hand-written naive loops; benchstat output; Go version not stated in README (internal/asm/go.mod says go 1.24.0)
hardware: 13th Gen Intel Core i9-13900 (AVX2) and Apple M2 Pro (arm64 NEON)
tradeoffs: AVX2 required on amd64 (runtime dispatch, AVX variants also generated) and NEON on arm64; pure-Go fallback via purego tag; amd64 and arm64 only; function-call overhead dominates tiny slices (Go never inlines asm).
caveats: Baseline is a deliberately naive byte loop; the stronger comparison is the uint64-wise purego column (asm about 3x faster on Popcnt-32 and 8x on And-32, geomean about 5x, derived from the page's sec/op rows). Assembly is emitted by avo programs in internal/asm (a Go DSL), not typed as a raw .s file. Throughput rows are +1000% to +2000% over naive, so quote the purego column for a fair comparison. Very small repo (2 stars).
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/avx2?l=go topic listing, then README and benchmark.sh

name: vectorcmp (hexon)
baseline: pure-Go scalar loop that sets one bit per matching element (build tag purego), compiled by the Go gc compiler
workload: comparison of a search value against a fixed-size array of uint8/16/32/64 and float32/64 producing a bit-packed result mask (equals, not-equals, greater/less than, greater/less or equal) with AVX2 VPCMP
claimed_speedup: sec/op, purego vs avx2: VectorEquals8 145594.5ns -> 628.0ns (-99.57%, about 232x derived from page data); VectorEquals16 151.078us -> 1.325us (-99.12%); VectorEquals32 146.441us -> 2.626us (-98.21%); VectorEquals64 146.577us -> 4.468us (-96.95%); VectorGreaterThan8 146456.5ns -> 856.9ns (-99.41%)
compiler_and_flags: go test benchmarks compared with benchstat (n=10, p=0.000); Go toolchain version not stated in README (go.mod says go 1.18); purego tag selects the baseline
tradeoffs: amd64 AVX2 only, with runtime detection and a pure-Go fallback; result is a packed bitmask, so callers must consume bitmaps; array sizes fixed by the benchmark.
caveats: The baseline is a naive scalar Go loop doing a read-modify-write on the output byte per element, not a SWAR or hand-unrolled Go version, so the 97-99.6% reductions overstate the gain over good scalar code. Assembly is produced by internal/avo (asm_amd64.s header says 'Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT'), not typed by hand. README does not name the Go version or array length. The Go Reference badge points at github.com/Jille/vectorcmp, so the import path may differ from this repo.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/avx2?l=assembly topic listing, then README and file listing

name: gocrack (wa7nt)
baseline: Go standard library crypto/md5 and crypto/sha1 (single-stream hashing)
workload: hashing short candidates (up to 55 bytes, one padded block) for brute-force and wordlist password recovery, 8 candidates per AVX2 register (multi-buffer), 1 core
claimed_speedup: md5x8 kernel alone 48 MH/s vs crypto/md5 5.7 MH/s (about 8.4x, derived from page data); sha1x8 compare path 22 MH/s vs crypto/sha1 4.1 MH/s (about 5.4x, derived); whole MD5 brute-force pipeline 38 MH/s on 1 core and 151 MH/s on 4 threads; kernels at 88-90% of a measured ALU-op ceiling
hardware: Intel Core i5-7360U (Skylake, 2 physical cores, AVX2, no AVX-512, no SHA-NI)
tradeoffs: AVX2-only, Skylake-tuned 8-lane kernels; only single-block messages (55 bytes or less); multi-buffer design raises throughput over many independent candidates but does not speed up one hash; x86-64 only.
caveats: The stdlib rows come from an ad hoc comparison: crypto/md5 is used only for self-verification in internal/md5x8, and no stdlib benchmark harness is visible in the repo. An 8-lane multi-buffer kernel against single-stream stdlib code is not a like-for-like latency comparison. No LICENSE file in the repo listing (usability set to reference). Two commits, one star. Password cracking tool (its README states authorised-use only).
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/avx2?l=assembly topic listing, then README, internal/md5x8/md5x8_amd64.s

name: Constantine (inline x86-64 assembly field arithmetic)
language: Nim (C, Rust and Go bindings; x86-64 inline assembly emitted by Nim macros)
baseline: the same big-integer / finite-field code compiled without assembly (CTT_ASM=0) by GCC and Clang
workload: finite field arithmetic on BLS12-381 (6 limbs) and elliptic-curve primitives using MULX, ADCX and ADOX carry chains that compilers cannot generate
claimed_speedup: 'The speed improvement on finite field arithmetic is up 60% with MULX, ADCX, ADOX on BLS12-381 (6 limbs)'; '2.4x perf ratio between using plain GCC vs GCC with inline assembly'; Clang/MSVC/ICC generate code 'up to 20~25% faster than GCC' for add-with-carry code
compiler_and_flags: CC=clang nimble bench_* recommended; GCC used for the 2.4x comparison; compiler versions not stated
hardware: plots are PNG files named R7_7840U (Ryzen 7 7840U, inferred from file names); BN254 MSM plot on i9-9980XE (18 cores, 4.1GHz all-core turbo)
tradeoffs: Assembly only on x86-64 (ARM has none yet); fastest path needs BMI2 and ADX; Nim toolchain with C ABI; Intel assembly syntax is unsupported by Apple Clang; constant-time guarantees are the stated reason for inline assembly.
caveats: The 60% and 2.4x figures are prose claims; the page shows benchmark plots as images and no numeric table or side-by-side comparison with blst or mcl. The 2.4x ratio is GCC-specific (the page says GCC is about 50% slower than Clang on the pure path). Nim inline assembly is generated by a macro DSL rather than a .S file.
found_via: GitHub: README.md and README-PERFORMANCE.md of mratsim/constantine, checked as a cryptography library with x86-64 inline assembly

name: wasm-fun (hand-written WebAssembly text algorithms)
baseline: the same skeleton-tracing algorithm compiled from C with Emscripten to WebAssembly, and a vanilla JavaScript implementation
workload: traceskeleton: topological skeleton of a binary image returned as polylines (includes its own malloc and linked list); other modules are thinning, distance transform, contour finding, maze generation
claimed_speedup: traceskeleton.wat '~300% faster than the version complied with emscripten (and ~10x smaller), ~500% faster than vanilla Javascript'
tradeoffs: Algorithms must be written directly in WAT (assembled with wabt); binaries average about 900 bytes; manual memory management with a small malloc; no toolchain dependency.
caveats: Single README sentence with no benchmark script, browser or engine, hardware, Emscripten version or flags, or input size; the tests folder holds usage examples, not timing code. '300% faster' is ambiguous (3x or 4x). Public-domain dedication carries no patent grant.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github hand-written WebAssembly text (WAT) kernel faster than Emscripten compiled C benchmark'

name: go-memset (tmthrgd)
baseline: Go gc compiler output for the loop 'for i := range data { data[i] = value }' (BenchmarkGoSet); also compared with the runtime-optimised zeroing loop (BenchmarkGoZero)
workload: memset of a byte buffer with an arbitrary value, sizes 32 B to 512 MiB
claimed_speedup: Memset vs Go loop: 32 B 5060.69 vs 1840.05 MB/s; 1k 44788.18 vs 1878.82 MB/s (about 24x, derived from page data); 16k 58868.04 vs 1896.63 MB/s (about 31x); 512M 15305.03 vs 1894.31 MB/s (about 8x). Parity with the runtime's zeroing loop: 16k 58868.04 vs 58854.20 MB/s
tradeoffs: x86-64 assembly only; generic Go fallback on other architectures (memset_other.go); function-call overhead for tiny buffers.
caveats: No CPU model or Go version stated; numbers date from a 2016-2019 Go toolchain, so modern Go may behave differently. At 32 B and 1k the runtime's own zeroing loop (GoZero 9326.33 and 53557.45 MB/s) is faster than this memset. Repository archived by the owner.
found_via: GitHub: README of tmthrgd/go-memset, from the tmthrgd Go assembly package family (go-hex is catalogued elsewhere)

workload: test whether every byte of a slice equals a given value, sizes 32 B to 512 MiB
claimed_speedup: README speedup table (old Go loop to go-byte-test): 32 B 5.02x, 128 B 15.45x, 1K 34.02x (1177.11 -> 40050.28 MB/s), 16K 42.28x, 1M 24.66x, 512M 14.77x

name: go-popcount (tmthrgd)
language: Go (x86-64 POPCNT assembly, popcnt_amd64.s and popcount_amd64.s)
baseline: Go loop over math/bits.OnesCount64 (BenchmarkCountBytesGo and BenchmarkCountSlice64Go)
workload: population count over byte slices and []uint64 slices, 32 B to 512 MiB
claimed_speedup: CountBytes vs Go math/bits loop: 32 B 5854.04 vs 2883.25 MB/s; 1K 20804.48 vs 8896.25 MB/s (about 2.3x, derived from page data); 16K 28642.76 vs 9986.94 MB/s (about 2.9x); 512M 11912.45 vs 7855.21 MB/s (about 1.5x)

name: fastxor (lukechampine)
baseline: naive byte-wise Go for loop and a word-wise (uint64) Go loop, compiled by the Go gc compiler
workload: xor of two byte slices (16 B, 1024 B and 65 KiB) and a specialised 16-byte Block function
claimed_speedup: 'fastxor is 2-40 times faster than a naive for loop'; AVX 65k 67217.99 MB/s vs byte-wise 1684.45 MB/s (about 40x, derived from page data) and word-wise 13203.25 MB/s (about 5x); 1024 B AVX 66089.39 vs byte-wise 1677.18 MB/s; Block about 6x faster than Bytes (13546.30 MB/s)
tradeoffs: x86-64 AVX/SSE assembly with generic Go fallback (xor_unaligned.go); Go never inlines assembly, so tiny slices lose most of the gain.
caveats: No CPU model or Go version; the author calls it a first try at writing Go assembly; small repo with 12 commits; the headline 40x is against a byte-wise loop, the word-wise baseline gives about 5x.

name: xhex (templexxx)
baseline: Go standard library encoding/hex (scalar byte loop)
workload: hex encode and decode of byte slices from 16 B to 2 KiB
claimed_speedup: 'typical results': Encode/16 5.25x, Encode/24 2.44x, Encode/1024 28.54x (1793 -> 62.8 ns/op); Decode/32 5.75x, Decode/48 2.48x, Decode/2048 19.92x (3634 -> 182 ns/op)

name: minio/highwayhash (Go assembly for amd64, arm64 and ppc64le)
language: Go (assembly for Intel AVX2, ARM NEON and SVE, ppc64le)
baseline: the package's own non-optimized pure-Go HighwayHash (Go gc output) on ppc64le; Go crypto SHA-256, SHA-512, SHA-1, MD5 and Blake2b for cross-algorithm context; upstream claim vs SipHash
workload: HighwayHash 64/128/256-bit sums and Write on messages from 16 B to 25 MB, single core
claimed_speedup: ppc64le accelerated vs non-optimized: Write_8K 531.19 -> 5566.41 MB/s (10.48x), Sum64_8K 9.58x, Sum256_8K 8.90x; Skylake Xeon Platinum 8124M, 5 MB messages: HighwayHash 11986.98 MB/s vs SHA256_AVX512 3552.74, Blake2b 972.38, SHA1 950.64, MD5 684.18, SHA512 562.04, SHA256 383.07 MB/s; README states HighwayHash is 'approximately 5x faster' than SipHash (no numbers)
compiler_and_flags: Go >= 1.11 required for the assembly; Go version for the numbers not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7 3.1 GHz (Sum256 up to 14928.71 MB/s at 1M); EC2 c7g.4xlarge Graviton3 (Sum256 5621.73 MB/s at 10M); 3.0 GHz Xeon Platinum 8124M; ppc64le hardware not stated
tradeoffs: HighwayHash is a keyed PRF / fast fingerprint, not a drop-in SHA-2 replacement; separate hand-maintained assembly file per architecture (amd64 baseline and AVX2, arm64 including an SVE file, ppc64le); no code generator in the file listing.
caveats: The cross-algorithm table compares different hash functions; the ppc64le baseline is the unoptimized Go code, not a C reference; the 5x-vs-SipHash line is inherited from the upstream C++ project with no numbers on this page; Go version and ppc64le CPU not stated; the benchmark code for the cross-hash table lives in the separate fwessels/HashCompare repo (not opened).

name: aadomn/aes (fixsliced constant-time AES in Cortex-M and RV32I assembly)
language: ARM Cortex-M and RISC-V RV32I assembly, with C reference (opt32)
baseline: previous bitsliced and constant-time AES implementations on Cortex-M and RISC-V cited by the TCHES 2021 paper (not shown on the repo page); the repo's own portable C opt32 versions
workload: constant-time AES-128 and AES-256 encryption in cycles per byte on a Cortex-M3 and a SiFive E31 RISC-V core, fixsliced (2 blocks in parallel) and barrel-shiftrows (8 blocks) representations; first-order masked AES-128 on Cortex-M4
claimed_speedup: Paper title: 'New bitsliced AES speed records on ARM Cortex-M and RISC-V'. README table (cycles per byte): AES-128 fully-fixsliced 84.3 on Cortex-M3 and 89.3 on E31, semi-fixsliced 87.1 / 93.4, barrel-shiftrows 94.8 / 78.9; AES-256 fully-fixsliced 115.6 / 122.4; masked AES-128 199.3 (semi) and 195.8 (fully) on Cortex-M4. No baseline row on the page.
hardware: ARM Cortex-M3, SiFive E31 RISC-V core, Cortex-M4 (masked version)
tradeoffs: Fixsliced variants need only 352 bytes (AES-128) of round keys for 2 blocks in parallel; barrel-shiftrows needs 1408 bytes and 8 blocks; fully-fixsliced is faster but has larger code size; constant-time with no table lookups; separate assembly per ISA, aimed at 32-bit microcontrollers.
caveats: Repo page gives only the authors' own cycle counts; the comparison to earlier work is in the TCHES 2021/1 paper (peer-reviewed, eprint 2020/1123) which could not be opened here, so a verifier could lift this to tier B after reading the paper. The C opt32 directory is didactic and not benchmarked for comparison. The masked implementation has no practical security evaluation (README caution).
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/aes?l=assembly topic listing, then README

name: AVR-AES-faster (rgrgrg)
language: AVR assembly (.S files) with C/C++ wrappers
baseline: AVRAES (point-at-infinity.org, rijndaelfast.asm), Osvik et al. 'Fast Software AES Encryption', AVR CryptoLib, AVR-Crypto-Lib, the tiny version of uclouvain lightweight cipher code, and any pure C/C++ implementation
workload: AES-128/192/256 block encryption, decryption and key expansion on 8-bit AVR, cycle counts for the inline (no call overhead) assembly version
claimed_speedup: README says 'Seems to be faster than' the five listed AVR AES libraries and 'Any pure C/C++ implementation' (no competitor numbers on the page). Own table: AES-128 encrypt 2111 cycles (S-box in flash) or 1951 (S-box in RAM), decrypt 2687 / 2527, key expansion 748 / 708; tiny version (keys on the fly) 2949 encrypt, 3538 decrypt.
tradeoffs: Constant-time; 512 bytes of S-box tables (flash) or 688 bytes RAM in the RAM variant; tiny variant needs only 16 bytes RAM but overwrites the key in place and must roll it back; C ABI call adds about 140 cycles per block.
caveats: The faster-than claims against named libraries have no numbers on the page, so they cannot be checked from it; cycle counts exclude call overhead; baseline libraries are other AVR assembly, not compiler output.

name: Nettle (assembly for x86_64, arm64, powerpc64, s390x)
language: C with assembly (arm, arm64, powerpc64, s390x, sparc64, x86, x86_64 directories)
baseline: Nettle's own generic C implementations before the assembly was added (previous releases)
workload: symmetric crypto kernels in the NEWS file: AES-256-CTR and AES-256-GCM, Chacha on Power9; SHA-1 and SHA-256 with sha_ni on x86_64
claimed_speedup: NEWS 3.7: new PowerPC64 assembly, 'Benchmarked on a Power9 machine, speedup was 13 times for AES256-CTR and AES256-GCM, and 3.5 times for Chacha'; NEWS 3.5: x86_64 sha1/sha256 using sha_ni, 'Speedup of 3-5 times on affected processors'; NEWS 3.8: new ARM64 implementation of AES, GCM, Chacha, SHA1 and SHA256 'Great speedups' (no numbers)
hardware: Power9 for the 13x and 3.5x figures; x86_64 with sha_ni for the 3-5x figure (CPU models not stated)
stars_or_usage: 76 stars (GitHub mirror of the upstream repository)
tradeoffs: Fat builds (default since 3.7) select assembly at runtime by CPU feature; per-architecture assembly to maintain; copyleft licence (GitHub shows LGPL-3.0 and the repo carries COPYINGv2, COPYINGv3 and COPYING.LESSERv3).
